title: BVA Decision 25000009
text:
Citation Nr: 25000009
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 18-13 806
DATE: January 2, 2025

REMANDED

Entitlement to service connection for an acquired psychiatric disorder, to include post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), is remanded. 

Entitlement to a total disability rating based on individual unemployability (TDIU) is remanded. 

REASONS FOR REMAND

The Veteran served on active duty in the United States Army from April 1969 to November 1970. These matters return to the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) after they were remanded by the Board in December 2023. 

Although the Board sincerely regrets the additional delay, these matters must be remanded once again for additional development.

Entitlement to service connection for an acquired psychiatric disorder, to include PTSD.

In its December 2023 remand, the Board directed the Agency of Original Jurisdiction (AOJ) to schedule the Veteran for a VA examination to determine whether the Veteran suffers from a psychiatric disability due to his active-duty service. The remand specified that the examiner must specifically address the Veteran's July 2022 positive screening for PTSD.

Following a May 2024 VA examination, the examiner concluded that the Veteran did not suffer from PTSD or any other mental disability. In doing so, he acknowledged that the Veteran experienced various stressors, including witnessing shells firing overhead and artillery fire, and firing his weapon. However, he did not at all address the Veteran's July 2022 positive screen for PTSD nor did he indicate that the Veteran suffered from any mental health symptoms at all. Indeed, he left the entire lengthy list of mental health symptomatology unchecked. 

VA's duty to assist a veteran in substantiating his claim includes obtaining a medical examination when necessary and ensuring that it is adequate to decide the claim. See 38?U.S.C. §?5103A(d); see Barr v Nicholson, 21?Vet. App.?303, 312 (2007). An examination report is inadequate if it provides an incomplete analysis or if it does not consider all the relevant evidence of record. Stefl v. Nicholson, 21?Vet. App.?120 (2007); Nieves-Rodriquez v. Peake, 22?Vet. App.?295 (2008); Dalton v. Nicholson, 21?Vet. App.?23 (2007).

As the May 2024 examiner failed to provide an appropriate explanation for failing to diagnose the Veteran with any psychiatric disability, a remand is required.

Entitlement to a TDIU is remanded. 

On the same basis, this matter must also be remanded. Pursuant to the Board's remand, an Individual Unemployability statement was prepared in March 2024. However, it concluded, without any explanation whatsoever, that the Veteran is capable of performing sedentary work. It did not discuss what service-connected disabilities are implicated in the Veteran's employment limitations nor did it provide any rationale as to why sedentary work is possible, while physical work is not. 

A concurrent VA examination indicates that the Veteran's diabetes mellitus, type II, prevents him from doing strenuous work and that the Veteran is easily fatigued with pain, numbness and tingling. Also, he cannot walk or stand for long periods of time. This is consistent with a conclusion that the Veteran can nevertheless do sedentary work. 

However, another examination report indicates that the Veteran's bilateral upper and lower diabetic peripheral neuropathy has a "profound" impact on his work due to pain, tingling and numbness; and that it hinders the Veteran's physical ability but also his fine motor skills and coordination, potentially impacting activities that require precision and dexterity. It stands to reason that this would significantly limit the Veteran's ability to complete sedentary work.

Based on this, the Board finds that a remand is required for an addendum opinion that specifically addresses the impact of the Veteran's bilateral upper and lower peripheral neuropathy on his ability to do sedentary work.

The matters are REMANDED for the following action:

1. Schedule the Veteran for a psychiatric examination with a new examiner to determine the nature and etiology of any PTSD. The examiner must consider and specifically address the Veteran's July 2022 positive screening for PTSD. If the Veteran is diagnosed with PTSD, the examiner must explain how the diagnostic criteria are met and opine whether it is at least as likely as not related to a verified in-service stressor. 

If any other acquired psychiatric disorders are diagnosed, the examiner must opine whether each diagnosed disorder is at least as likely as not related to an in-service injury, event, or disease. 

2. Afterward, obtain a new Individual Unemployability statement that discusses the impact of all of the Veteran's service-connected disabilities and that specifically addresses whether and how the Veteran's upper and lower bilateral peripheral neuropathy affects his ability to participate in sedentary work. 

 

Wendy Daknis

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Freda J. F. Smith, Counsel

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.
